topics.title: Greetings and introductions
topics.intro: French greetings change with the time of day and with the person. Use **tu** with a friend, a child or a pet, and **vous** with an adult you don’t know well (or with more than one person). To introduce yourself, give your name, age and home town: Je m’appelle…, j’ai… ans, j’habite à…
topics.teach: Teach your grown-up how to greet a French friend and a French teacher, and explain why the words are different.
topics.talk: Pretend you are meeting for the first time in a French café. Say “Bonjour !” and ask {him} to tell you {her} name, age and home town in French. Then ask {him} what each part meant.
topics.hook: **tu** for a friend, **vous** for a teacher. Age uses **avoir**: j’ai douze ans, “I have twelve years”.
topics.example: In a French shop, say “Bonjour, madame” or “Bonjour, monsieur” as you walk in: not greeting the shopkeeper seems rude.

topics.title: Numbers and prices
topics.intro: Up to 69, French numbers work like English. Then French counts in twenties: 70 is soixante-dix (60 + 10), 80 is quatre-vingts (4 × 20) and 90 is quatre-vingt-dix (4 × 20 + 10). Prices are said euros first, then the cents: 3,50 € is trois euros cinquante.
topics.teach: Explain how to build 97 in French, and why 80 has an s but 81 does not.
topics.talk: Read out prices from a receipt (pretend the £ are €) and ask {him} to say them in French. Then ask {him} to say a phone number in French, in pairs of digits, as French people do.
topics.example: French phone numbers are read in pairs: 06 12 45 78 90 is “zéro six, douze, quarante-cinq, soixante-dix-huit, quatre-vingt-dix”.

head: French
how it works
visual.caption: Belgium and Switzerland say septante (70) and nonante (90), and parts of Switzerland say huitante (80).

topics.title: Days, months, dates and birthdays
topics.intro: Days and months have no capital letter in French. A date is **le** + number + month: le quatorze juillet. Only the 1st is different: le premier mai. To say “on Mondays” (every week), put le before the day: le lundi.
topics.teach: Say your birthday and three family birthdays in French, and explain why the 1st of the month is different.
topics.talk: Each morning this week, ask {him} “Quelle est la date aujourd’hui ?” and let {him} answer in French. Check against a calendar: you will hear the month.
topics.hook: **le + number + month**: le quatorze juillet. Only the 1st is **premier**. No capitals: lundi, mai.
topics.example: France’s national day is le quatorze juillet, linked with the storming of the Bastille prison in Paris in 1789.

head: English
French
visual.caption: No l’ before huit or onze. Days and months are masculine and have no capital letter.

topics.title: Telling the time
topics.intro: Quelle heure est-il ? Answer with Il est… heures. Up to half past, add the minutes: et quart, et demie, vingt. After half past, go to the next hour and take away: moins dix, moins le quart. Timetables use the 24-hour clock: dix-sept heures quarante.
topics.teach: Explain how to say 8:50 in French, and why it uses neuf (nine).
topics.talk: Ask “Quelle heure est-il ?” a few times today and let {him} answer in French; check the clock together. Then ask {him} to read three times from a TV guide or a train timetable, the 24-hour way.
topics.hook: **Past the half? Next hour, then moins.** 8:50 = neuf heures moins dix. heure is feminine: **une** heure, et demi**e**.
topics.example: French television’s main evening news is called “le vingt heures”: it starts at 20:00.

head: French
visual.caption: Midday is midi and midnight is minuit. Midi et demi has no e, because midi is masculine.

topics.title: Family and pets
topics.intro: The word for “my” matches the noun: mon père, ma mère, mes parents. Use il y a for “there is / there are”, avoir for what people have (j’ai un chien) and s’appeler for names: Mon frère s’appelle Tom.
topics.teach: Draw your family tree and label it in French with mon, ma and mes.
topics.talk: Look at family photos and ask “C’est qui ?” (who is it?). {She} answers in French, for example “C’est ma tante.” The table in this topic shows the words, so you can check.
topics.hook: **mon** père, **ma** mère, **mes** parents: “my” matches the person you are talking about, not you.

topics.title: Describing people
topics.intro: Hair and eyes take avoir: J’ai les yeux verts et les cheveux longs. Personality takes être: Je suis sportive. Adjectives agree with the person: add -e for a girl or woman and -s for more than one. Colours come after the noun.
topics.teach: Describe yourself and a friend in French, then explain why some adjectives changed their spelling.
topics.talk: Play “Qui est-ce ?” (Who is it?): {she} describes someone in the family in French and you guess who it is. Ask {him} what each describing word meant.
topics.hook: **Hair and eyes: avoir** (j’ai les yeux bleus, “I have the eyes blue”). **Personality: être**, with agreement: il est grand, elle est grand**e**.

head: he is…
she is…
visual.caption: Add -e for feminine unless the word already ends in -e. -if becomes -ive and -eux becomes -euse.

topics.title: School: subjects, opinions and the timetable
topics.intro: School subjects take le, la, l’ or les: le français, la musique, l’histoire, les maths. Give an opinion with a reason: J’aime l’histoire parce que c’est intéressant. Lessons on the timetable take à: à huit heures.
topics.teach: Tell your grown-up tomorrow’s timetable in French, with an opinion and a reason for two subjects.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for {her} favourite and least favourite subjects in French, and why (“Pourquoi ?”). Listen for parce que, “because”.
topics.hook: **Opinion + subject + parce que + c’est + adjective**: J’adore le dessin parce que c’est créatif.
topics.example: At many French collèges there are no lessons on Wednesday afternoon, so pupils do sport, music or clubs instead.

topics.title: Free time and sport
topics.intro: Use jouer à for sports and games (je joue au foot), jouer de for instruments (je joue du piano) and faire de for other activities (je fais de la natation). Say how often: souvent, parfois, le week-end.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between je joue au tennis, je joue du violon and je fais du vélo.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what {she} does after school and at the weekend, in French. Then ask {him} to teach you one French sentence about your own hobby.
topics.hook: **Jouer À for balls, jouer DE for music, FAIRE DE for the rest.**

head: verb
examples
rows: jouer à + a sport or game
je joue au foot, à la pétanque
je joue du piano, de la guitare
je fais du vélo, de la natation, de l’équitation
visual.caption: à + le = au, de + le = du.

topics.title: Food, drink and meals
topics.intro: Meals: le petit déjeuner, le déjeuner, le goûter (the after-school snack) and le dîner. For food in general use du, de la, de l’ or des (“some”): je mange du pain. After a negative, just de: je ne mange pas de viande.
topics.teach: Describe what you usually eat for each meal, in French.
topics.talk: At a meal, ask {him} to name everything on the table in French. Ask “C’est bon ?” (is it good?) and let {him} answer.
topics.hook: **du, de la, des = some**; **pas de** after a negative. A potato is une pomme de terre: an “apple of the earth”.

head: some
rows: pas de pain, pas de fraises

topics.title: At the café and the market
topics.intro: Order politely with Je voudrais… (I would like) and s’il vous plaît. Ask for the bill with L’addition, s’il vous plaît. Quantities take de: un kilo de pommes, une bouteille d’eau.
topics.teach: Act out ordering a drink and a snack at a café, then asking for the bill.
topics.talk: Be the waiter: say “Bonjour ! Vous désirez ?” (What would you like?) and let {him} order in French. Then {she} asks for the bill.
topics.hook: **Je voudrais** = I would like. A quantity takes **de**: un kilo **de** tomates, never des.
topics.example: In France the service charge is included in the bill (service compris), so a tip is a small extra, not expected.

topics.title: My town and directions
topics.intro: Say what is in your town with il y a (there is) and il n’y a pas de (there isn’t a). Ask the way with Où est… ? and give directions: tournez à gauche, tournez à droite, allez tout droit.
topics.teach: Give your grown-up directions in French from your front door to the nearest shop.
topics.talk: Hide a small object and let {him} guide you to it in French: à gauche, à droite, tout droit, stop ! Then swap: the table in this topic has the words.
topics.hook: **à droite** = right, **tout droit** = straight on: one letter apart, so listen carefully!

topics.title: Home and my bedroom
topics.intro: J’habite dans une maison or dans un appartement. Name the rooms (la cuisine, le salon, ma chambre) and say where things are: sur (on), sous (under), dans (in), à côté de (next to), devant (in front of), derrière (behind).
topics.teach: Describe your bedroom in French, saying where five things are.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to give you a tour of your home in French, naming each room. Then put an object somewhere and ask “Où est… ?” (where is…?).
topics.hook: **sur** = on (a surface), **sous** = under (un sous-marin = a submarine).

topics.title: Weather and seasons
topics.intro: Most weather uses il fait: il fait beau, il fait chaud, il fait froid. Rain and snow have their own verbs: il pleut, il neige. Wind and fog use il y a: il y a du vent. Seasons: en été, en automne, en hiver, but au printemps.
topics.teach: Give a French weather forecast for today and tomorrow, like a TV presenter.
topics.talk: Each morning, ask {him} “Quel temps fait-il ?” (what’s the weather like?) and let {him} answer in French by looking out of the window.
topics.hook: **Il fait** for most weather, **il pleut / il neige** on their own, **il y a du** for wind and fog. **Au printemps**, but en été, en automne, en hiver.

topics.title: Holidays and travel
topics.intro: Holidays bring the tenses together: je vais (I go), je suis allé(e) (I went), c’était super (it was great) and je vais aller (I am going to go). Transport: en for things you ride inside (en voiture, en train, en avion), à on foot or on a bike (à pied, à vélo).
topics.teach: Describe a past holiday in French: where you went, how you travelled, the weather and what you thought of it.
topics.talk: Look at holiday photos together and ask {him} to describe one in French. Prompt with: Où ? (where?) Avec qui ? (with whom?) Quel temps ? (what weather?) C’était comment ? (what was it like?)
topics.hook: **En inside, à on top**: en voiture, en train, en avion, but à vélo, à cheval, à pied.

English
visual.caption: Careful: un car is a coach, not a car (une voiture).

topics.title: Clothes, colours and shopping
topics.intro: Porter means to wear: je porte un jean et un pull. Colours are adjectives, so they come after the noun and agree with it: une robe verte, des chaussures noires. Marron and orange never change.
topics.teach: Describe what you are wearing today in French, with colours, and explain one agreement.
topics.talk: Point at clothes in a shop window or a wardrobe and ask {him} to name each one with its colour in French.
topics.hook: **Colours follow the noun and agree**: une robe vert**e**. **Marron** (a chestnut) and **orange** (the fruit) never change.

head: masculine
feminine
visual.caption: Add -s for the plural (des pulls noirs), except marron and orange.

topics.title: My daily routine
topics.intro: Daily routines use reflexive verbs, with an extra me (myself): je me réveille, je me lève, je m’habille. Put the day in order with d’abord (first), ensuite (then) and enfin (finally), and add the time: à sept heures.
topics.teach: Tell your grown-up your morning routine in French, with times and the words for first, then and finally.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to describe {her} morning in French while acting it out, and guess each action.
topics.hook: **me = myself**: je **me** lave, “I wash myself”. Before a vowel: je **m’**habille.

topics.title: The body and health
topics.intro: To say what hurts, use avoir mal à + the body part: j’ai mal à la tête, j’ai mal au ventre (à + le), j’ai mal aux dents (à + les). Je suis malade means I am ill.
topics.teach: Play the doctor: say three things that hurt in French, then give some advice.
topics.talk: Play “Jacques a dit” (Simon says) with body parts: read a French word from this topic, and {she} touches the right part of the body.
topics.hook: **J’ai mal à + body part**: à la tête, **au** ventre (à + le), **aux** dents (à + les).

topics.title: Media, technology and the internet
topics.intro: Say how you use technology: j’envoie des messages, je regarde des vidéos, je joue à des jeux vidéo. Give balanced opinions (c’est utile mais c’est dangereux) and stay safe online: il ne faut jamais partager ton mot de passe.
topics.teach: Give two advantages and two dangers of the internet, in French.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how {she} uses a phone, tablet or computer, in French, and what {she} thinks of social media (les réseaux sociaux).
topics.hook: **télécharger** = download (not charge!). **Une émission** is a TV or radio programme, not an emission.

items.explain: Bonjour is the everyday “hello”, from morning until early evening; it also means “good morning”.
Bonsoir = good evening. Bonne nuit (good night) is only for going to bed.
Salut is the friendly “hi”, and also “bye”: use it with friends, not with teachers.
À bientôt = see you soon. À demain = see you tomorrow; à plus tard = see you later.

items.prompt: How do you say **What’s your name? (to a friend)** in French?
items.explain: Comment tu t’appelles ? (or Comment t’appelles-tu ?) asks a friend’s name. Answer: Je m’appelle…
items.learn: **Comment tu t’appelles ?** = What’s your name? (to a friend)

items.explain: Je m’appelle means “I am called” (literally “I call myself”): my name is Léa.
items.learn: **Je m’appelle Léa.** = My name is Léa.

items.explain: Ça va ? = how are you? / how’s it going? The answer can be the same words: Ça va (bien) !

items.prompt: Your friend asks “Ça va ?” and you feel great. What do you say?

options.feedback: That means “so-so”.
That means “not very well”.

items.explain: Ça va très bien, merci = I’m very well, thanks. Add “Et toi ?” to ask back.
French uses avoir (to have) for age: j’ai douze ans, “I have twelve years”.

items.prompt: How do you say “I am twelve”?

options.feedback: Age uses avoir, not être: j’ai douze ans.
deux is two: you would be a toddler!
Age uses avoir and ans: j’ai douze ans.

items.explain: Age uses avoir: j’ai douze ans (I have twelve years). Ask: Tu as quel âge ? or Quel âge as-tu ?

items.prompt: How do you say **I live in London.** in French?
items.explain: Towns and cities take à: j’habite à Londres. Je becomes j’ before a vowel or a silent h: j’habite.
items.learn: **J’habite à Londres.** = I live in London.

items.prompt: How do you say “please” to a friend?

options.feedback: That is the polite form, for an adult or for more than one person.
merci beaucoup means thank you very much.

items.explain: s’il te plaît to a friend (tu); s’il vous plaît to an adult or a group (vous).

items.prompt: Which word for “you” do you use with your teacher?

options.feedback: tu is for one friend, a family member, a child or a pet.
toi is the tu form after a preposition: avec toi, et toi ?

items.explain: vous for an adult you don’t know well, and for more than one person. tu for a friend, family, a child or a pet.
Enchanté (enchantée if you are a girl) = pleased to meet you. Bonne journée = have a nice day; bienvenue = welcome.

items: Moi, je m’appelle Inès. Tu as quel âge ?
items.explain: A greeting and a question, the answer with a question back, another question, and an answer with goodbye.

items.prompt: In Belgium and Switzerland, 70 is “septante”. What do people say in France?

options.feedback: There is no such number: France says soixante-dix (60 + 10).
soixante-sept is 67.

items.explain: France says soixante-dix (60 + 10). Septante is used in Belgium and Switzerland.
quatre-vingts = four twenties = 80. The s goes when another number follows: quatre-vingt-un (81).

items.prompt: How do you say **21** in French?
items.explain: 21 = vingt et un: 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 (and 71) join the one with et.

items.prompt: Which of these numbers does NOT use **et**?

options.feedback: 71 does take et.
31 does take et.
51 does take et.

items.explain: Only 21, 31, 41, 51, 61 and 71 take et. 81 and 91 do not: quatre-vingt-un, quatre-vingt-onze.

items.prompt: How do you write 200 in French?

options.feedback: cent takes an s when it is multiplied and nothing follows: deux cents, but deux cent un.
une centaine means “about a hundred”.

items.explain: deux cents (200), but deux cent dix (210): the s goes when another number follows.

items.prompt: How do you say the year 2026?

options.feedback: English says “twenty twenty-six”, but French says “two thousand and twenty-six”.
mille never takes an s.
There is no et in it.

items.explain: deux mille vingt-six: two thousand + twenty-six. mille never changes.
C’est combien ? (or Ça coûte combien ?) = how much is it?

items.prompt: What does **Ça coûte deux euros.** mean?
items.explain: coûter = to cost. deux = 2, douze = 12, vingt = 20.
items.learn: **Ça coûte deux euros.** = It costs two euros.

items.prompt: How is three euros fifty written in France?

options.feedback: French uses a comma where English uses a decimal point.
That is three hundred and fifty euros!

items.explain: In France the decimal point is a comma, and the € usually comes after the number: 3,50 €.
There are 100 centimes in a euro. A coin is une pièce and a banknote is un billet.

items.prompt: Which is written correctly in French?

options.feedback: Days and months have no capital letters in French.
Months have no capital letter either.
Days have no capital letter.

items.explain: No capital letters for days or months (except at the start of a sentence): le lundi 3 mars.

items.prompt: How do you say “the 1st of May”?

options.feedback: The 1st is the only date that uses a different word: premier.
Dates are masculine: le premier.

items.explain: The 1st is le premier; every other date uses the plain number: le deux mai, le trois mai.

items.prompt: What does **Mon anniversaire, c’est le douze août.** mean?
items.explain: douze = 12 (deux = 2, vingt = 20), août = August (avril = April).
items.hear: Mon anniversaire, c’est le douze août.
items.learn: **Mon anniversaire, c’est le douze août.** = My birthday is on 12 August.

items.prompt: How do you say **When is your birthday? (to a friend)** in French?
items.explain: C’est quand, ton anniversaire ? Answer: Mon anniversaire, c’est le…
items.learn: **C’est quand, ton anniversaire ?** = When is your birthday? (to a friend)
accept: Quelle est la date de ton anniversaire ?

items.explain: mercredi = Wednesday. Careful: mardi is Tuesday.
items.hook: mardi (Mars), mercredi (Mercury), jeudi (Jupiter): the Roman gods hide in the days.

items.explain: jeudi = Thursday, Jupiter’s day. vendredi (Friday) is Venus’s day.

items.prompt: How do you say **August** in French?
items.explain: August = août, said “oot”. The circumflex replaces an old s.
items.hook: Many French circumflexes mark an s that has gone: août (from Latin augustus), forêt (forest), hôpital (hospital).

items.prompt: How do you say **June** in French?
items.explain: June = juin; July = juillet. Both start with ju-, so learn them as a pair.

items.prompt: Put the days of the week in order, starting with Monday.
items.explain: The French week starts on Monday: lundi, mardi, mercredi, jeudi, vendredi, samedi, dimanche.
juillet, août, septembre, octobre, novembre, décembre.

items.prompt: Which is correct for “the 11th of November”?

options.feedback: There is no l’ before onze (or huit): le onze, le huit.
French dates use plain numbers, except the 1st (le premier).

items.explain: le onze novembre. No elision before onze or huit.
aujourd’hui = today, demain = tomorrow, hier = yesterday.

items.prompt: “Le lundi, j’ai maths.” What does **le lundi** mean here?

options.feedback: For one particular day, French uses the day on its own: lundi, je vais au cinéma.
le lundi means every Monday.

items.explain: le + day = every week on that day: le samedi, je joue au foot (on Saturdays I play football).

items.prompt: How do you say **What time is it?** in French?
items.explain: Quelle heure est-il ? Answer: Il est… heures. (Quel temps fait-il ? asks about the weather!)
items.learn: **Quelle heure est-il ?** = What time is it?

options.feedback: heure is feminine, so it is une heure.
One hour, so no s on heure.

items.explain: Il est une heure (1:00), il est deux heures (2:00).
midi = midday (12 noon); minuit = midnight.
minuit = midnight; la nuit = the night.

items.prompt: Il est deux heures et demie. What time is it?

options.feedback: Half past two: French says the hour that has passed, then et demie.
et quart is quarter past; et demie is half past.

items.explain: et demie = half past: 2:30.
items.hear: Il est deux heures et demie.

items.prompt: Il est six heures moins le quart. What time is it?

options.feedback: That would be six heures et quart.
moins means minus: six o’clock minus a quarter = 5:45.

items.explain: sept heures du matin = 7 am; trois heures de l’après-midi = 3 pm; huit heures du soir = 8 pm.

items.prompt: What does **huit heures du soir** mean?
items.explain: du soir = in the evening: huit heures du soir = 8 pm (20:00).

items.prompt: Le train part à dix-sept heures. When does the train leave?

options.feedback: dix-sept is 17, not sept: 17:00 is 5 pm.
The 24-hour clock: 17:00 is in the afternoon.
dix-sept is 17: 17:00 is 5 pm.

items.explain: dix-sept heures = 17:00 = 5 pm. Take away 12 to change from the 24-hour clock.
items.hear: Le train part à dix-sept heures.

items.prompt: How do you say **at half past seven** in French?
items.explain: à = at. heure is feminine, so demie has an e: sept heures et demie.
items.learn: **à sept heures et demie** = at half past seven

options.feedback: That is Quelle heure est-il ?
That would be Pendant combien d’heures ?

mon frère = my brother; ma sœur = my sister.

items.prompt: How do you say **my parents** in French?
items.explain: mes is “my” for plurals, whatever the gender: mes parents, mes sœurs.

items.prompt: What does **Je suis fille unique.** mean?
distractors: I am the only girl here.
items.explain: fille unique (for a girl) or fils unique (for a boy) = an only child.
items.learn: **Je suis fille unique.** = I am an only child.

items.prompt: How do you say **I have a dog.** in French?
items.explain: chien is masculine: un chien. A cat is un chat.
items.learn: **J’ai un chien.** = I have a dog.

items.prompt: What does **Elle a deux chats.** mean?
items.explain: elle = she, il = he; deux = two, douze = twelve; un chat (cat), un cheval (horse).
items.learn: **Elle a deux chats.** = She has two cats.

items.explain: un lapin = a rabbit; un hamster; un cochon d’Inde (a guinea pig); un oiseau (a bird).

items.prompt: How do you say **a goldfish** in French?
items.explain: A goldfish is a “red fish”: un poisson rouge. Careful: un poison (one s) is poison!

items.prompt: Dans ma famille, il y a quatre personnes. What does **il y a** mean?

options.feedback: il y a is a set phrase meaning “there is” or “there are”.
I have is j’ai.

items.hear: Dans ma famille, il y a quatre personnes.

mon père is my father; mon frère is my brother.

mon oncle = my uncle; ma tante = my aunt.
ma cousine is a girl cousin; mon cousin is a boy cousin.

items.prompt: What does **J’ai les yeux bleus.** mean?
items.explain: les yeux = the eyes (one eye is un œil). Eyes and hair take avoir and les: j’ai les yeux bleus.

items.prompt: How do you say **I have short hair.** in French?
items.explain: les cheveux (hair) is plural, so courts takes an s. Careful: les chevaux are horses!
items.learn: **J’ai les cheveux courts.** = I have short hair.

grandes is for girls or women (feminine plural).

items.prompt: What does **J’ai mal à la tête.** mean?
items.explain: avoir mal à + body part = to have a pain in…: j’ai mal à la tête = my head hurts.
items.learn: **J’ai mal à la tête.** = I have a headache.

items.prompt: How do you say **I have a stomach ache.** in French?
items.explain: le ventre is masculine, so à + le = au: j’ai mal au ventre.
items.learn: **J’ai mal au ventre.** = I have a stomach ache.

items.prompt: What does **J’ai mal aux dents** mean?

items.prompt: What does **J’ai de la fièvre.** mean?
items.explain: la fièvre = a fever, a temperature; la grippe = flu; un rhume = a cold; la toux = a cough.
